Unabridged Travel Chaos

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On Monday new laws will come into place that will drastically effect our tourism potential

Summary:
From the 1st of June travelling in and out of the country with children under 18 is now only legal if you meet a whole set of new criteria.

Despite overwhelming evidence that the visa regulations have already caused irreparable harm – Home Affairs is pushing ahead with the implementation of requirements for all children to carry unabridged birth certificates, which is due to come into effect on 1st June.
The tourism sector, despite accounting for 9% of GDP and employing 1,5 million (directly employing over 600 000 )people, has not to date had any opportunity to put their case that there are alternative remedies available that cater for the aims Home Affairs is trying to achieve, but without harming one of the only sectors South Africa is currently winning in Moreover, despite having a year to get their act together, Home Affairs has only last week issued standard operating procedures on the birth certificates.
One thing appears inevitable: serious damage will be done to SA tourism and jobs will be lost


Further information:
"There has been no consultation with the industry to obtain its input. You would expect it in a fully functional democracy," says David Frost, Southern African Tourism Services Association CE.
Dept of Home Affairs, say these regulations are necessary to combat child trafficking, but there is no evidence that this will deter criminals. Child trafficking is a major problem around the world, but we are the only country who has conceived that this could be a solution, at the International Travel Conference in Berlin earlier this year, where Child Trafficking is an important issue, SA ‘s new regulations were laughed at. To date there has been no consultation with the major players in our tourism industry. "We had a promise of a government and industry task team but nothing came of it," says Frost. "There is also no economic impact study, something to be expected when an industry producing 9% of SA’s GDP is impacted."
Home Affairs minister Malusi Gigaba, promised a task team in October last year to look into the issues, but the task team has nevr met.
With the birth certificate deadline looming, nerves are on edge. "There has been no communication whatsoever on how it will be implemented," says Frost "There is utter confusion. People in international markets are also desperate for clarity."
20% of air traffic into SA is families – there is the very real danger of anything from a 10% - 30% decline in volumes from our core markets of USA and Europe. It will also impact our regional neighbours, as most tourism transits through OR Tambo and will be subject to the regulations. In addition 465,000 children cross our borders by land each year, Up to 70% do not have birth certificates – are we going to close our borders to these families? Or as it seems the case are those borders not going to be regulated.
Also looming are biometric visas, a good idea but for one glaring flaw. Applicants will have to apply in person at an SA diplomatic mission. This measure has serious implications for visitors from a number of countries, including China and India, until recently SA’s fastest-growing inbound tourism markets.
Harm is already evident in visitor numbers from China and India, markets also shaken by news of new visa requirements. Their importance to SA is significant. Between 2008 and 2013, the last period for which reliable data is available, arrivals from China grew by 274% to 151 847 and from India by 132% to 112 672.
"Our Chinese business has been devastated," says Cullinan Holdings CE Michael Tollman. "It collapsed by 70% in September and has not recovered. China was our strongest growth market; now it is our weakest."
David Frost CEO , SATSA sees one hope. It came in President Jacob Zuma’s February state of the nation address when he noted: "We will prioritise the review of visa regulations to strike a balance between national security and growth in tourism."

Press Release:


Tourism Chaos Looms
Controversial new visa regulations coming into effect next Monday have outraged the tourism industry. The new rules dictate that all children under the age of 18 travelling into, out of or through South Africa will have to be accompanied by an unabridged birth certificate and are intended to combat child trafficking. But tourism experts tell Carte Blanche that this red tape will have a devastating blow on tourism and the economy.


Script:


David: With this level of confusion, one word chaos
Otto: Its done they have cancelled the flights they are no longer coming to South Africa.
Carla: We are very happy to support government to find a solution but this is not the solution

LINK
`From tomorrow the new travel regulations for children will come into effect, every child entering or leaving South Africa will have to have an UBC the travel industry is up in arms and they are predicting absolute chaos

V/O 14 sec
An Unabridged Birth Certificate is a certified document, which has the particulars of both, if known, parents on it. Home Affairs Director- General Mkuseli Apleni is standing firm on this requirement.

DG: If you are coming from a country which needs a visa those kids don’t need to carry an UBC because it was already included at the time of application but if you are coming from a country that doesn’t need a visa I need an UBC.

V/O 13 sec
United Kingdom and America, are two of the main non -visa countries, whose citizens not only visit South Africa in high volumes but certainly don’t understand the need to carry supporting documentation.

Carla: I think the confusion is Visa versus passport.

V/O
As chairman of BARSA Carla De Silva is the voice of our airline industry

Carla: Around the world you do need to produce specific documentation to apply for a visa but not travelling with a passport nowhere in the world do you have to travel with UBC.
Devi: Nowhere in the world
Carla: 100 % sure, we’ve spoken to bodies like IATA, these are international industry bodies when an UBC is not expected when you are travelling with a passport

V/O 16 sec
So with Home Affairs saying one thing and Tourism Reps another what is the story? Its all in the wording, Home affairs are saying that we are not unique because a birth certificate is required in some countries as supporting documentation, when you apply for a visa,

David: There is no uniformity in birth certificates some countries don’t even have them.
DG : When you call it unabridged it’s the word we are using in South Africa but whatever you are calling it in your country that’s why in the advisory we issued we said an unabridged birth certificate or a similar document which is having these details.
LINK
Tourism accounts for 9% of South Africa’s GDP directly employing over 600 000 people its revenue we cannot afford to lose but it seems we are going to have to take the knock.

V/O 9 sec
And these new regulations coming on the back of Eskom and Xenophobia, is one knock too far says Standard Bank’s Chief Economist Goolam Ballim.

Goolam: The type of policy making that we have more recently seen emerge out of the state is hardly constructive and the UBC policy or regulations seems to be in that direction their seems to be a smarter to achieve a laudable outcome but not this.

David: I am angry because I have seen this thing grow and I have seen the absolute benefit that this sector has brought to a country and I have seen people work passionately day in and day out a lot of them small business’s in rural areas creating jobs and they are people whose business’s with a foul swoop and crass hand from Home Affairs who are going to be severely impacted on.

V/O 14 sec
CEO of the South African Services Tourism Association, David Frost has been working at promoting our in bound tourism for the last 20 years and today one and a half million people benefit from this industry

Devi: Can we afford this kind of drama?
David: Tourism is the only sector that’s really growing at the market so what we need to do is to make it easier and more affordable for people to come to this country and what we are doing the this whole process is exactly the opposite.

V/O 11 sec
On Friday, in the UK’s Telegraph’s on line poll, 61 % of people said they wouldn’t now visit South Africa. But does this concern our Home Affairs

DG We have past that bridge that says we need them they don’t need us.
Devi Don’t we need them don’t we need their $’s?
DG: What I’m saying is not at the expense of our security and expense of protecting our children.

LINK
There is no question that the intentions behind the new regulations to curb child trafficking is good but industry experts say this is not the solution.

David: Is he suggesting that every other country in the world is not concerned about child trafficking because no other country in the world has introduced the birth certificate model. Mexico tried this a couple of years ago and abandoned it after three months, Thailand has promulgated this but they have never enacted it and you have to ask yourself why?
Devi How can we solve problem of child trafficking?
David: I was at a International Conference in Berlin United Nations World Travel and Tourism an organisation has a specific child trafficking unit. It is chaired by the ex head of UNICEF. These are people that have busied themselves in their entire lives looking at the scurge. The head of Interpol’s unit was there. I stood up and said guys this is what South Africa is trying to do. I tell you something jaws dropped they looked at me as if we were barking mad.

Devi : According to UNICEF 465 00 children cross our borders in South Africa per year and between 50% and 70% of them their births are not registered. These new regulations do they also apply to land borders.
DG: Whether it is about maritime border post, land border post, airport post you need to produce an UBC and a consent.
Devi: So whether we are talking Beitbridge or OR Tambo the rules are going to be the same.
DG: Wherever it is.

V/O 9 sec
What tourism bodies were pressing for was engagement with Home Affairs, to be involved in coming to a solution to fight the scurge of child trafficking…
David In a fully functioning democracy where we as a major sector have not had one opportunity to put our case on the table
Devi: And they disagree with that, they say nonsense.
David: That is an outright lie.
Otto It was really our hope to engage with the department in addressing our concerns around the implementation of this new policy. A task team called to life, by the Minister of Home Affairs, to date that task team has never seen the light of day

V/O 9 sec
A frightening prediction of a 20 % decline in tourism translates into 10 Billion Rand loss…. came from a Grant Thornton economic report.

Michael: Every 7 tourists will create 1 job, one in 8 people work for the tourism industry. The numbers are huge in terms of potential job losses, 20 % is a massive impact on an economy.

V/O 6 sec
Michael Tollman is CEO of Cullinan Holdings, one of South Africa’s leading leisure and tourism groups.

Michael Here we are shutting a door and when you shut a door and kill a market if you’ve spent 20 years as we have building up a brand which we are so proud of we can destroy that in a week.

V/O 16 sec
An example of how serious the tourism crisis can play out was last year when Home Affairs announced they were planning to introduce Biometric Visas for Chinese tourists meaning they would have to apply in person for their South African Visa in either Shanghai or `Beijing.

Michael: It was announced it would be implemented in China in only two places in September and in September our numbers went down by 70%. It was our strongest growth market of all of our markets globally.
Devi: 70% is a big part of the market?
Michael: 70 % gone we saw the immediate impact in September when it was supposed to come in never went in but it created the damage.

V/O 8 sec
The standard operating procedures from Home Affairs issued on how to implement these regulations are also confusing the tourism industry.

Carla: The standard operating procedures that arrived from government only arrived last week, this week we received another 4 versions we have five different versions of the procedures but it is very vague it is not clear for example a family arrives in South Africa, lets say they are coming from Sofia in Bulgaria the government official ,is he trained to understand the language that’s the first thing secondly he’s going to turn them away and that is the question we are asking the government who is going to bear the costs of turning this family away.
DG: It’s the airlines, that’s what the countries of the world they do, so that’s what we have done we have communicated with them and they must comply.
Otto: Every airline is going to review this from an economic point of view if indeed the route is under pressure and they reach a statistic where the demand and uptake to and from South Africa drops to a point where it is no longer viable to travel to SA they will review this route and they will pull the flights.
David: Vic Falls is about to put in a major international airport that they can take the traffic. Air China has just The message that sends is am appalling one that a government will just legislate without consulting a major sector.

People in international markets are also desperate for clarity." 20% of air traffic into SA is families – there is the very real danger of anything from a 10% - 30% decline in volumes from our core markets of USA and Europe. It will also impact our regional neighbours, as most tourism transits through OR Tambo and will be subject to the regulations. In addition 465,000 children cross our borders by land each year, Up to 70% do not have birth certificates – are we going to close our borders to these families? Or as it seems the case are those borders not going to be regulated. Also looming are biometric visas, a good idea but for one glaring flaw. Applicants will have to apply in person at an SA diplomatic mission. This measure has serious implications for visitors from a number of countries, including China and India, until recently SA’s fastest-growing inbound tourism markets. Harm is already evident in visitor numbers from China and India, markets also shaken by news of new visa requirements. Their importance to SA is significant. Between 2008 and 2013, the last period for which reliable data is available, arrivals from China grew by 274% to 151 847 and from India by 132% to 112 672. "Our Chinese business has been devastated," says Cullinan Holdings CE Michael Tollman. "It collapsed by 70% in September and has not recovered. China was our strongest growth market; now it is our weakest." David Frost CEO , SATSA sees one hope. It came in President Jacob Zuma’s February state of the nation address when he noted: "We will prioritise the review of visa regulations to strike a balance between national security and growth in tourism."
